analysis.one_liner: Expands the child tax credit, makes it fully refundable, and pays it out monthly.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 173 cosponsors, all Democrats, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on day one and never received a markup, a vote, or any further action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the child tax credit to $3,000 per child and $3,600 for each child under six, make every family eligible for the full amount even if it owes no income tax, adjust the amount for inflation each year, and send it to parents in monthly payments instead of one annual tax refund. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it; it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023. [S1][S2][S3][S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Parents of children under 18, with the biggest gains for low- and moderate-income families. Under the existing credit, a family that owes little or no income tax gets a reduced amount or nothing; this bill makes the full credit available to every family with a qualifying child. Families would also receive the money monthly through the year rather than in a single refund check. [S2][S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children, especially low-income parents

how_it_helps.text: Makes the child tax credit fully refundable, so a family with little or no income tax liability receives the full amount rather than a reduced credit.
Raises the credit to $3,000 per child aged 6 through 17 and $3,600 (120% of that amount) for each child under 6, and indexes both amounts to inflation after 2021.

Requires the Treasury to set up a program of monthly advance payments, with an online portal families can use to update changes in children, marital status, or income, and reduces the risk of overpayment by reconciling advances against the final credit.
Adds a $500 credit for other dependents, such as older dependents and some non-child dependents, phaseable down at higher incomes.

Requires Treasury to pay U.S. territories, including Puerto Rico and the Northern Mariana Islands, amounts equal to the benefits their residents would have received, so families in the territories are not left out.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The bill text contains no provision raising revenue to offset the cost, so the expansion would be financed by additional federal borrowing borne by general taxpayers over time. Families who receive advance payments based on prior-year information and then have a smaller credit coming could owe some of it back at tax time, though the bill includes an online portal and reconciliation rules to limit that. [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers via the federal deficit

drawbacks.text: The bill has no pay-for: it amends the tax code to expand the credit without any offsetting revenue, so the full cost lands on the deficit. [S3]

The phase-down is unusually broad: the entire credit begins phasing out at $180,000 for couples and $130,000 for single filers, a lower threshold and a blunter design than the temporary version Congress actually enacted in 2021, which protected the increase for middle-income families up to much higher incomes. Some upper-middle-income parents would see their credit cut sharply. [S3]

Monthly advance payments are based on the prior year's tax return, so a family whose income or family size changed could receive too much during the year and owe it back when filing, a real hardship risk that the bill mitigates but does not eliminate. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and targeted: a fully refundable credit at this size is among the most direct anti-poverty tools available, and the monthly payment design puts money in parents' hands when bills come due rather than once a year. The main costs are the deficit-financed price tag, which the bill makes no attempt to offset, and the reconciliation risk for families with mid-year changes. A stricter critic would also note that the phase-down design claws the credit back at much lower incomes than a better-drawn version would. On balance the bill's benefits for families with children outweigh its costs, though it is not flawlessly drafted.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled it for a markup, and no vote was ever held in either chamber before the Congress ended. [S1][S5]

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced the American Family Act of 2021 on February 8, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day. [S1][S5]
The bill gathered 173 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat. [S4]
The action history shows no further activity of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — after the February 8, 2021 referral. [S5]
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without a vote in either chamber. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo did. The smaller, partially refundable existing child tax credit stayed in place, low-income families with children continued to receive reduced amounts or nothing, and the federal budget avoided the cost of the expansion.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The tax-code status quo, and the deficit

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 8, 2021 and recruited a large Democratic cosponsor list.

for.name: 173 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Democratic Whip and many committee members.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its February 8, 2021 referral — no hearing or markup was ever scheduled during the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; no vote on it was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: All 173 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Ways and Means chairmanship and the House floor schedule were both controlled by Democrats, so the bill's death was a matter of the majority choosing not to act rather than a recorded opposition vote.

industries.note: Monthly advance payments would shrink the large annual refund checks around which paid tax preparation and refund-advance products are marketed to low-income families. Getting the money monthly instead is a gain for families and a loss for that business model. [S3]
